title: Quarterback runs: designed runs, scrambles and sneaks (and how to log each in your drill)
html:
Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this morning: it still holds only one logged game (Eagles at Bears, Week 3, 0 saved snaps) and no review files, and the original football-film-room repository was again not reachable from this run (access denied: not configured for this session). So there's no new miss of yours to fix. This lesson covers a call that trips up almost everyone in the drill: when the quarterback ends up running, was it a run play or a pass play? It's live this week: Tommy Carr's legs won Michigan the Penn State game and got him the start against Indiana, and Kalshi prices Drake Maye to run in a touchdown tonight.

The big idea: the box score counts every quarterback run the same way, as a "rush." But there are three very different plays behind those numbers. Two are called runs (the designed run and the sneak). One is a called pass that broke down (the scramble). Your drill asks what the offense called before the snap, so the scramble is a PASS even though the stat sheet says rush.

White = offense (squares are linemen), yellow = defense. Solid arrows = blockers and receivers; dashed white arrow = the quarterback's path. Dashed horizontal line = line of scrimmage. Each panel's "Log" label is how to score it in your Film Room drill.

  1. Designed run (panel 1). The play is built for the quarterback to carry it. In a QB draw, the line first sets up like it's pass blocking, so the linebackers drop back into coverage; then the running back becomes a lead blocker through the A gap and the quarterback follows. Other designed runs: the QB power, and the read option from Lesson 21 when the QB keeps it. Log it as RUN.
  2. Scramble (panel 2). A pass play: the receivers run routes, the line pass-blocks. The edge rush collapses the pocket (Lesson 24), nobody is open, and the quarterback escapes and runs. Log it as PASS, because that was the call. In the drill review, a scramble you logged as PASS is a hit, even though the play shows up in the box score as a rush.
  3. QB sneak (panel 3). Third or fourth down and about a yard. The quarterback lines up under center, takes the snap and pushes straight ahead behind the center into the A gap (Lesson 32's map). It's the highest-percentage short-yardage play in football; the Eagles' "tush push" version, with teammates shoving from behind, is the famous one. Log it as RUN.

Pre-snap clues for each: a mobile quarterback in shotgun with one back beside him and a light box (Lesson 19) → designed run or read option is possible. Quarterback under center, tight formation, 1 yard to go → sneak. Empty backfield, receivers spread wide, 3rd and long → it's a pass, and any QB run will be a scramble.

Real examples:

  • Michigan 21, Penn State 18 (last Saturday): freshman Tommy Carr came in at halftime, went 5 of 7 for 47 yards and ran for 36 yards, including the winning touchdown. Michigan is starting him against Indiana (Sun 1:00 a.m. JST / Sat 9:00 a.m. PT, FOX) partly because a quarterback who can run gives a defense one more ball carrier to account for.
  • 49ers 23, Commanders 17 (Monday): the brief's pregame case leaned on Jayden Daniels running. He ran 4 times for 10 yards. San Francisco's rushers stayed in their lanes instead of flying upfield, which closes the scramble escape in panel 2; Daniels beat them with his arm instead (300 yards).
  • Patriots at Bears (tonight, Fri 9:15 a.m. JST / Thu 5:15 p.m. PT, Prime): Kalshi prices "Drake Maye: rushing touchdown" at about 20¢. With backup guards (Lesson 32), Maye is more likely to scramble than usual, and Chicago is missing linebackers T.J. Edwards (doubtful) and Jack Sanborn (out), the players who usually spy a running quarterback.
  • Eagles (Monday night): with Jalen Hurts out and Tanner McKee, a pocket passer, starting, expect far fewer designed QB runs and sneaks from Philadelphia, one reason the line moved 7.5 points (today's Market 101).

What it means for your bets: a quarterback's rushing-yards prop mixes designed runs (predictable: the coach calls them) and scrambles (unpredictable: they depend on the pass rush). Backup offensive lines and missing spy linebackers raise scramble yards; a disciplined rush that stays in its lanes lowers them, as Monday showed. And a "rushing yards" over for a quarterback is partly a bet that his passing plays break down.

Connecting the dots: Lesson 21 (option and RPO) is the designed-run family; Lesson 24 (pass protection) explains why pockets collapse into scrambles; Lesson 32 (the middle of the line) is the map for the sneak; Lesson 19 (count the box) tells you whether a designed QB run has room.

For your Film Room drill: (1) Empty or 3-wide shotgun, 3rd and 7+: call PASS; if the QB ends up running, it's a scramble and your PASS call was right. (2) QB under center, 1 yard to go: call RUN (sneak). (3) Mobile QB in shotgun, one back beside him, 6 or fewer in the box: lean RUN (draw or keeper). When you save a snap where the QB ran, add a note "scramble" or "designed" so the review can grade the call, not the stat line.

Video: search YouTube for "QB draw explained," "quarterback scramble vs designed run," and "tush push QB sneak breakdown," then watch tonight's Maye snaps: did he run because the play said so or because the pocket broke?

Practice it in Football Camp → (Station 7: Read the snap)

quiz.q: It's 3rd and 8, the offense is in an empty shotgun, and the QB ends up running for 12 yards because nobody was open. How should you log it?
o: PASS, because it was a called pass that became a scramble
RUN, because he gained a first down
quiz.w: The drill grades the call. Receivers ran routes and the line pass-blocked, so it was a pass play; the stat sheet calls it a rush, but your PASS call was right.

quiz.q: In a QB draw, why do the linemen first set up like they're pass blocking?
o: To make the linebackers drop into coverage before the QB runs
Because they don't know the play
quiz.w: The fake pass pulls linebackers back; then the running back leads through the A gap and the quarterback follows into the space they left.

quiz.q: Quarterback under center, 4th and 1, tight formation. What's the most likely play?
o: A QB sneak behind the center
quiz.w: The sneak is the highest-percentage play for a yard: the QB pushes behind the center into the A gap. Log it as RUN.

quiz.q: Jayden Daniels ran only 4 times for 10 yards Monday. What did the 49ers' rushers do to stop his scrambles?
o: Stayed in their rush lanes instead of flying upfield
quiz.w: Rushers who keep their lanes don't leave the open edge a scrambler escapes through (panel 2), so Daniels had to win with his arm.
